1:
Keil and Delitzsch open with the shape of the whole. This chapter and the next form a connected prophecy, as appears from their arrangement under a single introductory formula and from their contents, the promise concerning the mountains of Israel standing so opposed to the threat against the mountains of Seir as to form its obverse and completion, the very forms of expression alluding across from one to the other. They summarise the argument: the mountains of Seir shall be laid waste, because Edom cherishes eternal enmity and bloody hatred toward Israel and has coveted its land and blasphemed Jehovah, while the mountain land of Israel, despised by the heathen for its devastation and seized as booty, shall be inhabited and cultivated again. Gill places it in the same sequence from the other side, as following the prophecy of the shepherds and the goats of the flock and turning now to the destruction of the enemies of the church under the name of Edom.

Henry notes that Mount Seir had been mentioned before only as partner with Moab in one threatening, but is here condemned by itself and has woes of its own. The prophet must set his face against it boldly, and Henry draws the rule that those who have God against them have his word against them and the face of his ministers too, who dare prophesy no good to them but evil. The ground of the controversy he finds in an enmity rooted in the heart, a perpetual hatred reaching to the very name of an Israelite, the same hereditary malice that Esau bore to Jacob because he got the birthright and the blessing. The comparison turns against the descendants rather than the ancestor: Esau had been reconciled to Jacob and had embraced and kissed him, and we do not find that he ever quarrelled with him again, yet his posterity would never be reconciled to the seed of Jacob. Hence the warning that children imitate the vices of their parents sooner than the virtues.

The geographical and historical notes are shared out. Gill derives the name from Seir the Horite who first possessed the country and was succeeded by Esau and his posterity, and the prophet is bidden to turn his face towards Edom or Idumea and look sternly at it. Ellicott calls Mount Seir a poetical designation of the Edomites taken from the land they inhabited, and fixes it as the mountainous region between the Dead Sea and the Elanitic Gulf; Wesley says as much in a line. Gill asks how the prophet could address a people he was not among, and answers that he might send the prophecy to their ambassadors at Babylon or by letter; he names Dedan, Teman and Bozrah among the cities to be laid waste. Clarke supplies the date, reckoning the prophecy delivered about the time of the preceding one and some five years before the destruction of Idumea by Nebuchadnezzar, and reports the opinion of Calmet that two destructions are foretold, one by Nebuchadnezzar and another by the Jews after their return. He renders the threatened desolation literally as a desolation and a wilderness.

Whether Edom means more than Edom is raised at once. Clarke keeps to the history: where other nations should recover their liberty after the fall of the Babylonian monarchy, the Edomites should continue in bondage for their despiteful behaviour towards the children of Israel in the day of their calamity. Ellicott goes further: the earlier denunciation had their historical relations to Israel in view, while this one regards them also as representative of the hostility of the world to the covenant people, which he argues from the desolation of so small a province being set against the rejoicing of the whole earth, and from Edom being coupled with the residue of the heathen. Gill likewise takes them for the enemies of the church in general.
5:
The ground of the sentence is an old grudge. Gill traces it to the posterity of Esau against the posterity of Jacob, because the latter supplanted the former and got the birthright and the blessing, a grudge discovered in all ages and on every occasion that offered. Clarke sets the two brothers side by side, contending even in the womb and living generally in enmity, and finds the descendants keeping up the feud, but the Edomites implacable, seizing the moment when the Israelites were most beset by other enemies to make inroads and cut them off wherever they were found. He turns this into a judgment on the temper itself: to afflict the afflicted is cruel, scarcely of man, bad as he is; a man must be possessed by a malignant spirit when he wounds the wounded and insults over those already under the rod of God. Ellicott observes that enmity toward Israel is imputed to other neighbours as well, but that the hatred of Edom was deeper and coeval with its first ancestor, and its peculiar malignity is noticed elsewhere among the prophets.

Ellicott dissents on the wording of the charge. Blood, he says, is not in the original and should be omitted, since the verb means literally to pour out, so that the clause should be rendered that they scattered the children of Israel; and he fixes the time referred to as the overthrow of Jerusalem, both the great calamity and the moment when their iniquity had an end. Wesley reads the same phrase of the punishment that brought them to final ruin. Ellicott also finds a play upon the name in the sentence, the threat being not that they should be prepared unto blood but that they should be made blood, the name itself meaning red; and he notes the congruity of the punishment, that violence should come upon one who had loved rather than hated violence. Clarke puts it most plainly of all, that they loved blood and shall have blood, and illustrates it with an old story of a conqueror slain in an ambush with two hundred thousand men by a queen who cut off his head and threw it into a vessel filled with blood, bidding him satisfy himself with what he had thirsted for.

Gill takes the oath at the head of the sentence as a form in which the Lord swears by himself, because he could swear by no greater, and which he never uses except in matters of importance. Ellicott finds the cutting off of the traveller a striking feature of the doom, since the nomadic tribes of Edom had been the great carriers between India and the East and Egypt and had grown rich by that commerce, whereas the fierceness of the few tribes now wandering there makes even the visit of a curious traveller a matter of difficulty and danger. Wesley glosses the phrase simply of all travellers going to or from Edom, and Ellicott adds that the rivers named are river courses in which water was found only at times. Gill sees the mountains filled with the slain of those who flee there for refuge, and reads the perpetual desolations as cities never built or inhabited again, while Clarke gives the whole sentence in a line: perpetual desolation for perpetual hatred.
10:
The second charge is covetousness. Ellicott marks the division: earlier the sin laid to Edom is hatred of Israel, here the desire to possess its inheritance. Gill offers two readings, either Idumea which Edom already held together with Israel which he hoped for, or, as he prefers, the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah, which he pleased himself would fall to him as next heir, the posterity of his brother being dispossessed. Clarke settles for the two kingdoms, and says the Idumeans would have succeeded but that the Lord was there, which spoiled their projects and blasted their hopes. Ellicott makes that clause carry the weight of the charge: Edom desired the possessions of Israel not as it might have desired those of any other nation, but knowing this to be the peculiar inheritance given by God to his people, which it thought should have been its own as the elder branch, so setting itself in direct opposition to God.

Henry supplies the history and the motive. The church had complained of them already for setting on the Babylonians against Jerusalem, crying rase it, rase it, so inflaming a rage that needed no spur; here they are further charged with triumphing in the ruin of the city and saying with pleasure that the mountains of Israel are laid desolate. He observes that the troubles of the church prove the constancy of its friends and draw out the corruptions of its enemies, in whom there appears more brutish malice than one would have thought of. The triumph he traces to two roots: a sinful passion of anger, envy and hatred, that same perpetual hatred charged earlier, so that not being a match for Israel themselves they were glad when the Chaldeans did them the mischief; and a sinful appetite for the land, to which they thought they could make out a title for want of other heirs, reckoning that if the issue of Jacob failed they stood next in the entail.

The words of the boast are weighed. Ellicott would render the blasphemies rather as reproaches, which became constructively blasphemies under the circumstances, though he thinks it better not to push the meaning beyond what was intended; Gill, rendering the boasting as a magnifying against God, holds that what is spoken against the people of the Lord is taken as spoken against himself. Clarke fills in what was said: they exulted in seeing Judea overrun and rejoiced in the prospect of completing the ruin once the Chaldeans had withdrawn, declaring they would take those lands for their inheritance though they knew God had promised them to the Israelites. Gill takes the closing formula to mean that God is known by the judgments he executes, by good and bad alike, and Wesley glosses the judging as punishing.

The last verses set the desolation of Edom against a general rejoicing, and the voices differ over how wide that rejoicing is. Wesley reads the whole earth as the inhabitants of the countries round about, in peace and plenty; Clarke takes it of the land rejoicing in the restoration of the Jews and suggests the time is probably that of the Maccabees; Gill takes it broadly, of the world in general in peace and prosperity. Ellicott states the choice, allowing that Hebrew usage would bear the whole land of Israel but preferring the wider sense, since the thought is not confined to Edom: when all the earth shall rejoice in the salvation of God and be full of his knowledge, then Edom, the hostile power of the world, shall be desolate. Clarke closes with the rule he finds inculcated throughout the chapter, that others shall rejoice in thy downfall as thou hast rejoiced at theirs, so a man may in some sort make his own temporal good or evil: wouldst thou not be slandered, then do not slander; be merciful, and thou shalt obtain mercy.
